Citation: Neprash et al. Trends in Ransomware Attacks on US Hospitals, Clinics, and Other Health Care Delivery Organizations, 2016–2021. JAMA Health Forum. 2022.
Design and data: Cohort of 374 publicly identified US healthcare ransomware attacks in the THREAT database.
Key quantitative findings: Care delivery disruption documented in 166 attacks (44.4%); mean reported disruption duration 15.8 days; 32 attacks (8.6%) exceeded 2 weeks; electronic-system downtime in 156 attacks (41.7%).
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform duration scenarios, prevalence context, and the need for long-horizon sensitivity analysis.
Important limitation: Public reporting is incomplete and selective; unsuccessful attacks are not observed; findings do not identify control efficacy or network transition probabilities.

Citation: Neprash, McGlave, and Nikpay. Hacked to Pieces? The Effects of Ransomware Attacks on Hospitals and Patients. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy. 2026.
Design and data: Hospital ransomware database linked to Medicare claims using event-study methods.
Key quantitative findings: Hospital volume decreased 17%–24% in the initial attack week and recovered within 3 weeks; in-hospital mortality among patients already admitted at attack onset increased 34%–38%.
Permitted use in NAZE: Define held-out operational-pattern targets and justify modeling degraded care and multiweek recovery.
Important limitation: Claims-based hospital outcomes are not equivalent to modeled service availability; estimates should not be converted directly into asset-level probabilities.

Citation: Ghafur et al. A retrospective impact analysis of the WannaCry cyberattack on the NHS. npj Digital Medicine. 2019.
Design and data: Hospital Episodes Statistics analysis comparing activity during the WannaCry week.
Key quantitative findings: Infected hospitals experienced an approximately 6% decrease in admissions; 13,500 outpatient appointments were cancelled in infected trusts; estimated lost activity was £5.9 million; no mortality increase was detected.
Permitted use in NAZE: Provide a lower-severity operational-impact pattern and evidence that effects vary by incident and system resilience.
Important limitation: Single major event with a same-day kill switch; activity changes are not direct service-availability measures.

Citation: Dameff et al. Ransomware Attack Associated With Disruptions at Adjacent Emergency Departments in the US. JAMA Network Open. 2023.
Design and data: Before-and-after cohort of 19,857 visits at two urban academic EDs adjacent to four attacked hospitals during a month-long incident.
Key quantitative findings: During attack/recovery, adjacent EDs experienced increases in census, ambulance arrivals, waiting, patients leaving without being seen, length of stay, diversion, and time-sensitive stroke-care metrics.
Permitted use in NAZE: Validate that severe incidents can generate regional spillover and motivate a future multi-hospital layer.
Important limitation: Observational single-region study; does not isolate individual defense effects.

Citation: Abouk and Powell. Ransomware Attacks, ED Visits and Inpatient Admissions in Targeted and Nearby Hospitals. JAMA. 2024.
Design and data: Difference-in-differences study of 8 attacks disrupting 15 California hospitals, compared with 355 unattacked hospitals.
Key quantitative findings: At attacked hospitals, ED visits and inpatient admissions fell about 8% one week after attack and about 16% two weeks after; nearby ED visits increased about 7% by week 3; effects later returned toward baseline.
Permitted use in NAZE: Supply an independent time-varying activity-loss and spillover pattern.
Important limitation: Only disruptive attacks were included; post-2020 attacks were unavailable; activity changes are not identical to service loss.

Citation: Pham et al. Ransomware Cyberattack Associated With Cardiac Arrest Incidence and Outcomes at Untargeted, Adjacent Hospitals. Critical Care Explorations. 2024.
Design and data: Cohort comparing pre-attack, attack, and post-attack phases at two hospitals adjacent to an attacked system; 78 cardiac arrests.
Key quantitative findings: Total cardiac arrests increased from 21 before to 38 during attack; favorable neurologic outcome among out-of-hospital arrests decreased from 40.0% to 4.5% during attack, then increased after; incidence per 1,000 admissions did not significantly differ.
Permitted use in NAZE: Demonstrate why regional workload and patient outcomes matter and why causal claims must be cautious.
Important limitation: Small event count and one regional incident; associations may reflect concurrent changes and diversion.

Citation: Larsen et al. Continuing Patient Care during Electronic Health Record Downtime. Applied Clinical Informatics. 2019.
Design and data: Hybrid quantitative and qualitative study of a 300-bed hospital ransomware event with about 48 hours total downtime followed by 48 hours partial recovery.
Key quantitative findings: Laboratory turnaround time in available paper records increased by about 20 minutes (62%); interviews suggested some reporting delays extended for hours; manual workflows and incomplete documentation limited measurement.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform degraded-service structural scenarios, recovery sequencing, and the need to model workarounds rather than binary service loss alone.
Important limitation: Single facility; incomplete paper timestamps; observed process delay cannot be generalized to every service.

Citation: Larsen et al. Implications of electronic health record downtime: an analysis of patient safety event reports. JAMIA. 2018.
Design and data: Coded 76 EHR-downtime reports from 80,381 patient-safety reports.
Key quantitative findings: Laboratory events accounted for 48.7% and medication events 14.5%; 46% indicated procedures were absent or not followed; only 27.6% indicated successful execution.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform service dependencies, manual-workaround failure modes, and uncertainty around downtime procedures.
Important limitation: Voluntary reports are selective and cannot estimate event incidence or capacity fractions.

Citation: AHRQ. Evidence-based Contingency Planning for Electronic Health Record Downtime: Final Report. 2018.
Design and data: Archival data, observations, 17 staff interviews, and coupled agent-based/discrete-event simulation at two hospitals.
Key quantitative findings: Among 76 downtime reports, 48.7% involved laboratory processes; 46% indicated procedures were absent or not followed; models used 1,500 iterations and showed benefits from workload reduction and additional staff.
Permitted use in NAZE: Provide a methodological example for triangulation, distribution fitting, and process-level downtime modeling.
Important limitation: Downtime data were incomplete and comprehensive downtime-model validation was not possible.

Citation: Ghayoomi et al. Assessing resilience of hospitals to cyberattack. Digital Health. 2021.
Design and data: Patient-based, resource-constrained discrete-event simulation of a typical urban tertiary hospital over a 16-day attack and recovery period.
Key quantitative findings: Simulated ransomware scenarios reduced patient throughput; ICU recovery lagged ED recovery; results compared recovery strategies rather than asset-level prevention portfolios.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform a future patient-flow layer, a longer recovery horizon, and healthcare simulation reporting.
Important limitation: Synthetic attack parameters and modeled strategies do not validate NAZE transition probabilities.

Citation: Willing et al. Simulating the overload of medical processes due to system failures during a cyberattack. BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. 2025.
Design and data: Hybrid discrete-event and agent-based model of emergency trauma processes and medical-device outages.
Key quantitative findings: In its sample scenario, CT outage up to 30 minutes had limited modeled effect; a 120-minute outage increased process duration about 47%, and 230 minutes increased it up to 128%.
Permitted use in NAZE: Provide an external structural check that operational effects are nonlinear with outage duration.
Important limitation: Proof-of-concept sample hospital; modeled results are not universal clinical thresholds.

Citation: Arsalani et al. Impact of ransomware on emergency medical services: empirical estimation and risk assessment framework. Omega. 2026.
Design and data: Empirical analysis of two Alabama hospital breaches plus an EMS simulation framework.
Key quantitative findings: The two incidents had different effects on ambulance performance; surrounding hospital capacity helped explain the difference.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform a regional capacity extension and reinforce that one incident pattern is not universal.
Important limitation: Full parameter details require full-text review; two incidents limit generalization.

Citation: Chiaradonna et al. Framework for cyber risk loss distribution of hospital infrastructure: Bond percolation on mixed random graphs approach. Risk Analysis. 2023.
Design and data: Probabilistic graph-theoretical model of loss across attacks on a prototypical hospital network.
Key quantitative findings: Derives mean and variance of aggregate loss under a mixed random-network model.
Permitted use in NAZE: Provide a comparable structural model and alternative topology/loss framework.
Important limitation: Prototypical network and theoretical loss model do not empirically calibrate NAZE.

Citation: Carramiñana et al. Enhancing healthcare infrastructure resilience through agent-based simulation methods. Computer Communications. 2025.
Design and data: Agent-based model coupling healthcare infrastructure and IT dependencies.
Key quantitative findings: Models cyberattack-driven IT degradation and downstream healthcare-service effects under parameterized severity and recovery.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform explicit interdependency modeling and multi-layer validation methods.
Important limitation: Sensitivity to configured attack severity is not external validation.

Citation: Wunderlich et al. Resilience against IT attacks in hospitals: results from an exercise in a German university hospital. 2023.
Design and data: Three-day hospital tabletop exercise following eight months of process mapping and fallback-plan development.
Key quantitative findings: Only 34% felt preparedness was sufficient; IT-specific plans increased from 1.7% of units before preparation to 86.7%; paper/offline-capable units appeared more resilient.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform a 72-hour scenario, workaround mechanisms, and expert-review questions.
Important limitation: One university hospital and self-reported assessments; not a source of control efficacy probabilities.

Citation: Angler et al. Assessing the impact of technology partners on the level of cyberattack damage in hospitals. Health Policy and Technology. 2025.
Design and data: Discrete-event simulation of downtime cost, length of stay, staff utilization, and lost arrivals in a general-hospital ED.
Key quantitative findings: Modeled 21-day scenarios and reported cost-benefit estimates for a technology-partnership intervention.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform economic-analysis structure and operational outcomes, not NAZE cost values.
Important limitation: Scenario-specific modeled costs and intervention assumptions are not transferable as procurement estimates.

Citation: Walsh, Borycki, and Kushniruk. Strategies in Electronic Medical Record Downtime Planning: A Scoping Study. 2019.
Design and data: Scoping review of four included downtime-planning articles.
Key quantitative findings: Identified four recurring themes: communication, procedure review/revision, system availability, and staff preparation.
Permitted use in NAZE: Inform control taxonomy and missing human/organizational mechanisms.
Important limitation: Only four included articles and no quantitative efficacy estimates.

Citation: Monks et al. Strengthening the reporting of empirical simulation studies: Introducing the STRESS guidelines. Journal of Simulation. 2018.
Design and data: Reporting guideline for discrete-event, system-dynamics, and agent-based simulations.
Key quantitative findings: Provides structured checklists for conceptualization, implementation, experimentation, data, and results reporting.
Permitted use in NAZE: Use as the reporting and reproducibility checklist.
Important limitation: Complete reporting does not itself establish validity.

Citation: CISA and partners. #StopRansomware Guide. 2023.
Design and data: Authoritative operational guidance.
Key quantitative findings: Recommends timely patching, least privilege, segmentation, offline/encrypted/tested backups, incident response planning, logging, and coordinated isolation.
Permitted use in NAZE: Define portfolio components and explicit failure modes.
Important limitation: Guidance does not quantify causal effectiveness.

Citation: HHS. Healthcare and Public Health Cybersecurity Performance Goals.
Design and data: Healthcare-specific authoritative guidance.
Key quantitative findings: Prioritizes high-impact safeguards for healthcare organizations.
Permitted use in NAZE: Define feasible healthcare control portfolios and terminology.
Important limitation: Voluntary goals do not provide transition probabilities or cost estimates.

Citation: NIST IR 8374 Revision 1. Ransomware Risk Management: A CSF 2.0 Community Profile. 2026.
Design and data: Authoritative ransomware risk-management profile.
Key quantitative findings: Organizes preparation, protection, detection, response, and recovery practices, including segmentation and tested recovery.
Permitted use in NAZE: Trace portfolio components to current risk-management practice.
Important limitation: Framework guidance is not empirical effectiveness evidence.
